verdict.failure_analysis: Trials 1 and 3 passed every hidden case. Trial 2 failed simple-ul, ol, existing-count-overwritten, omitted-li-closers, nested-list-counts-direct-children, incomplete-token-after-closed-list, and unsupported-after-closed-list for the same root cause: after a successful scan it called $processor->seek('1') even though no public bookmark named '1' had been set. That produced PHP warnings inside WP_HTML_Processor::seek() and crashed before next_tag()/set_attribute() could run. This is a bookmark-model misconception, likely encouraged by the rendered private $bookmark_counter passage saying generated bookmark names start at 1, plus the seek() section not explicitly saying the name must be a currently active bookmark created with set_bookmark(). The omitted-closer and nested-list cases were not primarily depth misunderstandings: trial 2 used the documented direct-child depth test. The after-closed incomplete/unsupported cases also show the intended policy was mostly understood: stop scanning when the first list ends, so later bad markup should not block the edit. The crash happened only when it tried to rewind via the nonexistent bookmark.

verdict.failure_analysis: No hidden case failed in this round: all three trials passed 8/8 cases and execution.json reports no _doing_it_wrong records. The rendered docs appear to have supported this task well. The main helpful passages were: html-tag-processor.md > Which processor should I use, which directs tree/text/omitted-closer work to WP_HTML_Processor; html-processor.md > create_fragment(), which identifies body-fragment parsing and its nullable return; html-processor.md > next_token(), which explains text-bearing token walks, implied structure such as synthesized TBODY, single-cursor state-machine traversal, and virtual closers; html-processor.md > get_current_depth(), which explicitly shows the >= depth-boundary pattern; and html-processor.md > Recipe: collect DOM-style text from a subtree plus get_modifiable_text(), which prevented the common mistake of appending comments, script/style text, or raw entity text. Near-misses were small: every trial omitted an explicit clean-scan policy for truncated or unsupported input, and two trials added an unnecessary is_tag_closer() guard after next_tag('TABLE'), suggesting those details are documented but could be made more prominent.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs mention synthesized TBODY and implied structure, but do not explicitly show optional table row/cell end tags producing virtual TR/TD closers. This is a general table-parsing contract, not specific to this task.

verdict.failure_analysis: All trials passed all 8 hidden cases, so there were no failed hidden cases to attribute to documentation gaps. The rendered docs did especially well on the critical distinctions for this task: the processor-selection guidance says to use WP_HTML_Processor for structure, missing/implied closing tags, and normalized output; the rewrite-while-serializing recipe and serialize_token() docs describe accumulating token output and wrapping serialize_token(); get_modifiable_text() documents decoded text for #text nodes; and the ordinary-text guidance warns that comments, attributes, and special-element opener text are not ordinary #text descendants. Those passages map directly to the entity, comment, attribute, split-node, and normalization cases. The near misses were around fallback policy and special elements: trial-2 and trial-3 still used normalize( $html ) ?? $html in an error branch after building rewrite output, and trial-3 defensively read special-element opener text even though it did not need it. These did not affect the hidden cases, but they show where the docs could make the successful pattern more obviously complete.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs warn that normalize( $html ) after a token loop discards emitted changes, but candidates still used it in error branches as a generic fallback.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a short contract-oriented fallback note: once a token rewrite has emitted output, fallback to normalize() or raw input is an explicit decision to discard the rewrite; string-returning filters should document whether they return best-effort accumulated output, an empty string, null, or the original input on unsupported markup.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs explain that SCRIPT/STYLE/TITLE/TEXTAREA text is carried on the opener token, but may leave readers thinking they must call get_modifiable_text() on those openers to preserve or skip the content.
doc_gaps.suggestion: State explicitly that no read call is needed to advance past or serialize special-element contents: serialize_token() on the opener preserves the token, and a #text-only filter naturally excludes opener-carried special text.

doc_gaps.problem: Processor creation failure and later parser aborts are documented separately, but examples leave fallback policy to the caller, which can produce inconsistent normalized-vs-raw behavior in string APIs.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Include a compact example of a string-returning API choosing one fallback policy consistently for both create_fragment() returning null and get_last_error() becoming non-null, without implying that raw input is normalized output.

verdict.failure_analysis: No hidden case failed in any trial. The docs did well in the exact areas this task required: the Tag Processor 'Which processor should I use?' section identifies flat position-based tag edits as Tag Processor work; 'Finding tags' documents both string and array next_tag() query forms; the next_tag() method docs state tag-name matching is ASCII case-insensitive and tag-like text in comments is never matched; the set_bookmark() docs explicitly describe the common 'last matching tag' pattern by re-setting the same bookmark on each match; add_class() documents creating or appending the class attribute without removing existing classes; and get_updated_html() is documented as the output path for queued edits. Near-misses were minor: all trials used release_bookmark() before get_updated_html(), which works, but release_bookmark() does not explicitly say that releasing navigation state does not affect queued edits. The implementations also do not inspect paused_at_incomplete_token(), but for this task the documented behavior is acceptable: incomplete trailing tags are not matched, and prior complete H2 tags can still be bookmarked, sought, and modified.

doc_gaps.problem: The docblock explains that releasing a bookmark frees overhead, but does not explicitly distinguish bookmark navigation state from queued document edits.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a sentence that releasing a bookmark does not undo, flush, or affect updates already enqueued on a token; callers should still use get_updated_html() to retrieve edits.

doc_gaps.problem: The docblock mentions a maximum seek limit but gives little practical guidance on when seeking to a bookmark is valid after a scan reaches false/end or pauses on incomplete input.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Document the normal post-scan use case: after next_tag()/next_token() returns false, callers may still seek to an existing bookmark unless a documented failure condition applies, such as a missing bookmark or seek limit.

doc_gaps.problem: The overview table clearly shows the string shorthand, but the method-level parameter description is dense and does not plainly restate that next_tag('img') is shorthand for array('tag_name' => 'img').
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a short method-level sentence with that equivalence and the case-insensitive matching rule so generated API references remain self-contained.

verdict.failure_analysis: All trials passed all 7 hidden cases, so there are no failed hidden cases to attribute to documentation failures. The rendered docs did well on the core decision points: the Tag Processor overview says to use it for flat attribute/class edits and byte-precise preservation, while the HTML Processor docs say structure-aware parsing is for containment, subtree walks, and normalized serialization. The Tag Processor usage section gives the exact create -> next_tag() -> modify -> get_updated_html() shape. get_attribute_names_with_prefix() documents lowercase names and case-insensitive matching, which explains the uppercase-source-attribute case. next_tag() documents that tag-like text inside comments and raw text is not matched, which explains comments-untouched. get_updated_html() documents that queued updates are applied while every untouched byte is preserved, preventing normalize()/serialize() misuse. Near misses: the docs imply but do not prominently state that a matched tag with no prefix matches returns an empty array rather than null, and remove_attribute() itself does not say that removal preserves surrounding whitespace, which matters for byte-exact expectations.

doc_gaps.problem: The return contract says array|null and gives an example for matches and for no matched tag, but does not explicitly distinguish 'matched tag with zero matching attributes' from 'no current tag opener'.
doc_gaps.suggestion: State that the method returns an empty array when a tag opener is matched but no attributes match the prefix, and returns null only when no tag opener is currently matched.

doc_gaps.problem: The method docs do not state that attribute-name matching/removal is ASCII case-insensitive or that lowercased names returned by get_attribute_names_with_prefix() are safe to pass directly.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a sentence that remove_attribute() matches attribute names case-insensitively in HTML parsing mode and accepts the lowercased names returned by get_attribute_names_with_prefix().

doc_gaps.problem: The byte-preservation behavior for removals is described generally under get_updated_html() and a future-direction note, but not at the removal method where users make the choice.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Mention that removing an attribute removes the attribute span but preserves surrounding source bytes, so extra whitespace around the removed attribute may remain by design.

verdict.failure_analysis: No hidden case failed in any trial: all three execution.json files report 7/7 passes and no _doing_it_wrong records. The docs did well here because they directly guided the required shape: the processor-choice text says to use WP_HTML_Processor for normalized output and missing/implied closing tags; create_fragment() is documented for BODY fragments; next_token() says it visits text plus tag openers/closers and emits closers for unclosed ordinary elements; serialize_token() says concatenating token serializations reconstructs normalized HTML, and its example removes an element while keeping contents by skipping matching tag tokens. Near-misses were limited to error policy: trials 1 and 2 used normalize($html) after a token rewrite if get_last_error() is set, which the docs warn will abandon skipped/wrapped/replaced tokens. No provided case exercised unsupported-markup abort behavior, so this did not affect functional results. Attribute null/true/empty-string semantics and decoded-vs-raw text semantics were not materially involved because the candidates did not inspect attributes or rebuild text; serialize_token() handled canonical encoding.

doc_gaps.problem: The method doc says it returns the uppercase name of the matched tag, but does not explicitly state the closer and non-tag behavior that makes trial-2's get_tag()-only predicate safe.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a sentence: when matched on either an opening or closing tag token, get_tag() returns that element name; when matched on text, comments, doctype, or no token, it returns null. Note that this is appropriate when a rewrite wants to skip both opener and closer tokens.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs warn that normalize($html) discards emitted rewrites, but the fallback examples still leave room for models to treat normalize($html) as a generic post-loop recovery path.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a small error-policy table distinguishing fail-closed, return accumulated best-effort output, and abandon-the-transformation fallbacks. State plainly that normalize($html) is only for intentionally abandoning every token-loop change and is not a transformed-output fallback.
